title: Visual Controls for the Home
subtitle: The homes are assigned and well placed, but silent, obvious only to the person who built them. A visual control makes each home explain itself, so anyone can find a thing and put it back at a glance, without asking.
part_position: Third chapter of Part Four (Straighten), chapters 12 to 15; continues the second of the six S's and takes the third Straighten step
hands_off_note: Chapter 14 makes each already-placed home speak for itself with a visual control, but a stranger can put any single thing away correctly and still have no idea how the whole house fits together, because they meet each home alone. Chapter 15 completes Straighten by giving the household one shared map of where everything lives, so the whole room can be read in a single look.
audience: Readers who have finished Chapters 12 and 13, given every keeper a home and placed each home by how often they reach for it, and are standing at the entryway where every home is now well chosen and well placed but completely unmarked, so only the person who built it knows what belongs where. Busy home keepers and parents. Applying the method, not new to it. They do not need to re-assign homes or re-place them by frequency; they need to make each silent home explain itself, so anyone can find a thing and put it back at a glance, without asking.
core_promise: Take the third Straighten step by making each already-placed home self-explaining with a visual control, so the rule for what belongs there moves out of one person's head and onto the shelf, where everyone can read it. Learn what a visual control is (any simple cue that makes the answer plain without a person, a conversation, or a list), judge every spot by the Glance Test (could someone who has never lived here put this away correctly, at a glance, without opening it, reading a list, or asking?), and use three simple cues, a label, an outline, and a boundary, plus seeing-in and color. Give each entryway keeper a voice, then scale the same cues to the pantry, the kids' zone, the junk drawer, and the linen closet, so the room keeps answering questions even when you are not there to answer them, all without adding or removing a single thing.
emotional_purpose: Keep the lighter Straighten mood going and lift a weight off the reader. A silent home is a design gap, not a family's failing; nobody failed, the knowledge was simply never written down anywhere the thing itself can be seen. The reframe, you were the label, is meant to relieve, not to scold: if a room only holds together when you personally tend it, that is why, and a cue on the shelf takes that standing duty off you. Deliver the honest third-Straighten-step milestone without overselling it: the room got easier even though nothing left the house, and the goal is still ahead.
practical_purpose: Show why a home can be placed perfectly and still leave everyone guessing (the rule lives in one person's memory); define a visual control and the shadow-board image that names it; teach the Glance Test as the hero check, clause by clause (at a glance, without opening it, without reading a list, without asking); teach the three simple cues (the label names what belongs, and you label the spot not just the thing; the outline shows the shape or place and its empty form reveals a missing item; the boundary shows the edges of a home and when it is overfull) plus the two lighter cues (seeing in, a clear jar or bin that shows contents and level; color, one shade per person or per kind); match one cue to the one confusion a spot keeps producing, and stop there; deliver the reframe that you were the label; walk the entryway keepers into voices (keys a labeled hook or painted silhouette, leash a labeled hook or outline, umbrella a control by its shape, bags a labeled basket, mail a tray marked out), then scale to the pantry, kids' zone, junk drawer, and linen closet; and read the friction meter as the third Straighten step.
primary_cta: Pick one bin, drawer, or shelf whose contents are a mystery from the outside, and give it one label or one clear container. Then ask someone else in the house to put a thing away there. If they get it right without asking, the home just started speaking. Read the chapter free in the online book.
secondary_cta: Read the chapter free online, then continue to Chapter 15, where Straighten finishes: each home now speaks for itself, but a newcomer still has to walk the whole house discovering them one at a time, so the next chapter gives the household one shared map of where everything lives, so the whole room can be read at once.
keywords: how to label storage so anyone can find things

hero_device: The visual control (the home that speaks)

worked_example.space: the settled, well-placed entryway from Chapters 12 and 13, where every keeper has a good home in the right spot but every home is completely unmarked, so the only person who can use the room without guessing is the person who built it; now each home is given a way to explain itself. Nothing moves in this pass; only the cues are added.
worked_example.note: The entryway is one small hallway, but the same three cues scale to every room in the house, and the busier the room, the more they repay. Nothing is added or removed; the homes just learn to explain themselves, so the room stops leaning on a single person's memory to run.

items.keys: The smallest cue that works: a single labeled hook, or better, a little key shape painted or drawn behind the hook, so the outline sits empty and obvious whenever the keys are out, and a house-sitter learns in one look where the keys live and whether they are home.
items.leash: The same idea, a hook marked leash or a simple drawn outline of it, so the friend walking your dog returns it to the hook instead of the counter, without being told and without guessing.
items.umbrella: The easy one, and the best lesson in the chapter: an umbrella stand needs no label at all, because its shape already tells you what it holds. The stand is a cue built into the object's own home, so whenever a container's form declares its job you get the control for free.
items.reusable_bags: Forever wandering off, they get a labeled basket or a hook that simply says bags, so all at once they have a place that claims them back.
items.outgoing_mail: A tray marked out, or to post, so the go-mail sits plainly apart from the keep-mail, and the letter you meant to send stops disappearing into the pile you meant to file.

worked_example.scaling_up: The pantry, where labeled bins and clear jars let you read the whole shelf without touching it and a single buy-more line drawn inside the rice jar tells you to restock the moment you can see past it; the kids' zone, where one color of hook and cubby per child sorts coats and bags before anyone is old enough to read the words; the junk drawer, where a cheap divider tray gives every small thing a bounded slot, so a tangle becomes a set of quiet compartments; and the linen closet, where a labeled shelf edge, sheets here, towels there, means a folded stack lands in the right place even when the person folding has never once put laundry away in this house.
worked_example.tally: Same keepers, same room, nothing added or removed, but each home now carries its own answer, so a pet sitter, a weekend guest, or a child can find a thing and put it back at a glance without ever reaching for the phone to ask. The room did the explaining, and it holds together even when the person who built it is somewhere else entirely.

definition: A visual control is any simple cue, a label, an outline, a color, a boundary, a clear container, that makes it obvious at a glance what belongs in a spot and whether it is there. It moves the rule out of your memory and onto the thing itself, so the home works even when you are not there to run it.
one_idea_to_keep: A good home does not need you to explain it. Put the knowledge where the thing lives, a label, an outline, a clear jar, and the room starts telling everyone what belongs where, so keeping order stops being your job alone.
key_motifs: the third chapter of Part Four (Straighten); it continues the second of the six S's and turns from placing homes well to making each placed home explain itself

a self-explaining chapter, not an assigning or placing one: the homes are already assigned (Chapter 12) and well placed (Chapter 13), and none of that unwinds here; this chapter only gives each home a way to speak

the starting gap: a home can be well chosen and well placed and still keep its knowledge to itself, because the rule for what belongs there sits in exactly one place, your memory, so the room runs beautifully when you are there to run it and quietly comes undone when you are not
a silent home is a design gap, not anyone's failing; the knowledge exists, it has just never been written down anywhere the thing itself can be seen

the hero device, the visual control: any simple cue attached to a spot that makes the answer plain without a person, a conversation, or a list, lifting the rule out of one person's memory and onto the thing itself
the frozen rule: a visual control makes the right thing obvious without a word

the shadow board from the workshop, the classic example: each tool has its own painted silhouette, so a glance shows where everything goes and one empty shape shows at once what is missing; referenced lightly and home-scaled

the secondary device, the Glance Test: could someone who has never lived here put this away correctly, at a glance, without opening it, reading a list, or asking? Every clause does work, and without asking is the heart of it

the three simple cues, each answering a different question: the label names what belongs (label the spot, not just the thing); the outline shows the shape or place and its empty form reveals a missing item; the boundary shows the edges of a home and when it is overfull

two lighter cues to fold in: seeing in (a clear jar or bin shows the contents and the level without opening) and color (one shade per person or per kind, read faster than any word, so a child who cannot yet read knows which hook is theirs)
matching the cue to the question is most of the skill: ask what the spot keeps getting wrong, add the one cue that answers it, and stop there, because a busy cue is one more thing to read past

the reframe: you were the label; the system lived in your head, so the room only worked when you were there to run it, and a control on the shelf takes that standing duty off you, including you on a tired day

the worked example gives the entryway keepers a voice, keys a labeled hook or painted silhouette, leash a labeled hook or outline, umbrella a control by its own shape, bags a labeled basket, mail a tray marked out, then scales to the pantry, the kids' zone, the junk drawer, and the linen closet

the umbrella's lesson: the best control is sometimes built into the object's home, so whenever a container's form declares its job you get the control for free, with nothing to print and nothing to draw

the fences: do not re-assign homes (Chapter 12), do not re-place by frequency (Chapter 13), do not map the whole room (Chapter 15), do not build routines or standards for keeping order (the later Standardize S), and do not re-open Sort
